newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Most LatAm shrs seen firm this wk on foreign buys.
newsitem.headline: Most LatAm shrs seen firm this wk on foreign buys.

text.p: Equities in most Latin American bolsas are seen firm this week as demand from foreign investors should continue driving share prices higher, analysts and brokers said.
However, re-election worries in Brazil and labor concerns in Venezuela could weigh on stocks in those countries, despite foreign interest, they noted.

Mexican shares are seen posting further gains this week, with analysts citing two main factors behind the market's rally -- foreign demand and a likely drop in interest rates during the second government auction of securities in 1997.
Last week Mexico's .IPC index closed at 3,596 points, with a rise of 2.98 percent.
In Chile, where the blue-chip .IPSA index jumped 3.9 percent in the last five sessions, foreign investment was also seen as key to bolstering the market's uptrend.
"The bolsa should hover at these levels but much will depend on the flow of orders from abroad," one dealer said.
A wave of buy orders from New York sparked a rally on the bolsa early last week, but the gains were soon undermined by a bout of profit-taking in the last two sessions, analysts said.
The blue-chips Merval index .MERV jumped 3.5 percent last week to close Friday at 674.93, a new high of nearly three years.

Trend for Brazilian bolsas, which also had been consolidating gains on foreign buying, would depend on the government's response to the PMDB party's vote against the re-election amendment, analysts said.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso suffered a blow in his campaign to run for a second term on Sunday when the biggest party in Congress voted to delay a constitutional amendment that would allow his re-election. Argentine stocks were also seen firm this week but could lose some of their recent momentum as investors pause and regroup following a long string of gains, analysts said.
Players turned more cautious Friday in view of erratic swings on Wall Street and a jump in U.S. long bond yields following the release of stronger-than-expected jobs data, they said.
"The local market might come under some selling pressure, especially if volatility mounts on Wall Street," said Andrs McKiguan at Velox traders. "But the underlying tone is firm."
The market reacted with disappointment early Monday but analysts said investors should absorb the news.
"It was a setback, but not the end of the world. There is a long way to go (before the re-election is approved)," said Craig Barley, from Rio de Janeiro-based bank Banco Omega.
Last week the Sao Paulo bourse's Bovespa index .BVSP of the most 49 traded stocks ended up 6.8 percent to 74,783 points.
In Venezuela, equities were seen weakening as labor problems look to continue, grabbing newspaper headlines and underlining one of the government's main policy challenges for the year, traders said.
Doctors and nurses voted last Thursday to suspend a 13-day strike that has seen wards and emergency rooms deserted throughout the country.
But this week may see teachers join a growing nationanl wave of protests over public sector pay levels.
Last Friday, the market's leading .IBC index closed down four percent at 6,837 points.
((--Fatima Cristina, Sao Paulo Newsroom, 5511 2485412))
